Title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act)
Who wrote it: The European Parliament and the Council of the European Union, under the ordinary legislative procedure, on a proposal from the European Commission (opinions from the European Economic and Social Committee, the European Central Bank and the Committee of the Regions are recited).
Date: Adopted 13 June 2024; published in the Official Journal of the European Union, L series, 12 July 2024 (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj).
What it is: An EU regulation (binding legislation, directly applicable in Member States), 'Text with EEA relevance'. The held copy is the Official Journal text (144 pages), extracted from PDF. It opens with numbered recitals (non-operative statements of reasons, mostly worded 'should'), followed by the operative articles and annexes. Coder A coded part 1 only: lines 1-2105, covering the citations and Recitals (1)-(158), pp. 1-40. Recital (158) begins in range at line 2092 and was read to its end at line 2129. The articles and annexes are in parts 2 and 3, coded by other agents.
What it is for: Per Recital (1): 'to improve the functioning of the internal market by laying down a uniform legal framework in particular for the development, the placing on the market, the putting into service and the use of artificial intelligence systems', promoting 'human centric and trustworthy' AI while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights, and supporting innovation. Per Recital (26) it follows a risk-based approach: it prohibits certain practices, sets requirements for high-risk AI systems and obligations for operators, and sets transparency obligations for certain AI systems. The recitals also cover general-purpose AI models, sandboxes and real-world testing, and the EU and national governance and enforcement set-up.
Other important notes: Binding regulation, but the part coded here is recitals: they explain and interpret the operative articles and do not themselves impose duties. All part 1 entries are therefore marked 'statutory: AI Act Recital (N) (non-operative)' with level 'non-binding interpretation (recital)', or 'n/a (provided)' for resources. Article cross-references in notes are marked [inference] because the articles were not in this part. Whom it applies to: providers and deployers, including public bodies (Recital 13: a deployer includes 'a public authority, agency or other body'; Recital 23: EU institutions, bodies, offices and agencies acting as provider or deployer; Recital 156: the European Data Protection Supervisor is their market surveillance authority). Duties along the value chain reach general-purpose AI model providers and suppliers (Recitals 85-88, 97-117). Public-sector-specific points in the recitals: fundamental rights impact assessment for deployers that are bodies governed by public law or private entities providing public services (96); registration of public-authority deployers in the EU database before use (131); high-risk areas covering public benefits and services, emergency calls, law enforcement, migration and asylum, justice, education, employment and critical infrastructure (54-62); an option for public authorities to fold quality management into national or regional systems (81); a power for law enforcement and civil protection authorities to deploy unassessed high-risk systems with authorisation sought afterwards (130). Exclusions and carve-outs: military, defence and national security (24); sole-purpose scientific research (25); tax, customs and FIU administrative proceedings are not law-enforcement high-risk uses (59); the non-public database section for law enforcement, migration, asylum and border uses (131); post-market monitoring excludes law-enforcement deployers' sensitive operational data (155); a law-enforcement exception to informed consent in real-world testing (141); two-person verification may be disapplied by Union or national law in law enforcement, migration, border control and asylum (73); Ireland and Denmark are not bound by certain law-enforcement provisions (40-41). Passages that bear on checking AI outputs: human oversight with authority to intervene or stop (73); two-person verification of biometric matches (73); no adverse legal decision based solely on a remote biometric identification output (35); final judicial decision-making must remain human (61); deployers must inform affected persons and tell them of their right to an explanation (93); AI-generated text published on matters of public interest must be disclosed unless it has had human review or editorial control (134); machine-readable marking and detection of synthetic content (133), which also bears on bodies checking incoming content. Extraction notes: the text comes from pypdf, so footnotes and running headers (e.g. 'OJ L, 12.7.2024 EN') sit between lines, and footnote markers such as '(38)' appear inside sentences. Quotes keep the text as extracted. No unreadable passages were found in lines 1-2129.

Title: Commission Guidelines on prohibited artificial intelligence practices established by Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act) — Communication from the Commission, C(2025) 5052 final
Who wrote it: European Commission (Brussels). The text says the drafting was informed by a stakeholder consultation organised by the Commission (providers and deployers, civil society, academia, public authorities, business associations), and that the Member States within the AI Board and the European Parliament were consulted (para 6).
Date: 29 July 2025 (dated 'Brussels, 29.7.2025'). The prohibitions it interprets apply from 2 February 2025 (para 3).
What it is: Commission interpretive guidelines on Article 5 of the AI Act, adopted under Art. 96(1)(b) of the AI Act. They run to about 135 printed pages in 12 sections: 1 background; 2 overview, material and personal scope, exclusions (national security, third-country cooperation, R&D, personal use, open source), interplay with high-risk rules, general-purpose AI and other Union law, enforcement and penalties; 3 Art. 5(1)(a)-(b) harmful manipulation, deception and exploitation of vulnerabilities; 4 Art. 5(1)(c) social scoring; 5 Art. 5(1)(d) individual crime risk prediction; 6 Art. 5(1)(e) untargeted scraping of facial images; 7 Art. 5(1)(f) emotion recognition; 8 Art. 5(1)(g) biometric categorisation; 9 Art. 5(1)(h) real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement; 10 safeguards and conditions for the RBI exceptions (fundamental rights impact assessment, registration, prior authorisation, notification, national laws, annual reports); 11 entry into application; 12 review and update.
What it is for: To increase legal clarity and give the Commission's interpretation of the Art. 5 prohibitions 'with a view to ensuring their consistent, effective and uniform application' (para 4). It is meant as practical guidance to help competent authorities enforce the prohibitions, and to help providers and deployers comply with them.
Other important notes: Binding status: the guidelines themselves are non-binding, and only the CJEU can give an authoritative interpretation (para 5). The prohibitions they interpret are binding law (AI Act Art. 5). The examples are 'merely indicative', and each case needs its own assessment (para 7). Whom it applies to: providers and deployers of AI systems, which explicitly include public authorities, agencies and other bodies (paras 16-17). An in-house system built by a public authority counts as 'putting into service' (para 13). Responsibility as deployer sits with the organisation, not with individual officials (para 18). The social scoring prohibition applies whether the system or score is provided or used by public or private persons (para 170). Many worked examples involve public bodies: tax authorities, social welfare and labour agencies, municipalities, migration authorities and police. Enforcement: market surveillance authorities designated by Member States, and the European Data Protection Supervisor for EU institutions (para 53). Whether public authorities can be fined is left to national rules (para 55). EU institutions can be fined up to EUR 1 500 000. Points that bear on checking AI outputs: human assessment combined with an AI score does not remove a system from scope if the score plays a 'sufficiently important role' (para 161); hallucination is not in itself deception where the provider has disclosed limitations and built in safeguards, outside sensitive contexts such as health, education and elections (para 73); providers and deployers must be able to show market surveillance authorities that a scoring system is 'performing as intended' and uses only relevant data (para 171); providers may monitor for misuse (para 41). Coding scope: part 1 (text lines 1-2945) covers sections 1-4.4 (paras 1-183). Sections 5-12, including all the RBI safeguards, are in part 2. Coding approach (coder A's own judgement): the document mostly restates and interprets AI Act provisions. Coder A coded these restatements as the document's official content, recording the statutory basis where the passage gives one. Expectations that come only from the Commission ('expected', 'should', 'encouraged') are marked non-statutory. Interplay passages that only report what other instruments require were mostly not coded. Extraction: the text was extracted with pypdf, so spacing errors (e.g. 'wi ll', 'deplo yers') are kept in the quotes.

Title: Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government
Who wrote it: Government Digital Service (GDS) ('Created by the Government Digital Service'). Foreword by Feryal Clark MP, Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for AI and Digital Government, DSIT; preface by David Knott, Government Chief Technology Officer, DSIT. The Acknowledgements credit input from central government departments (including CCS, Cabinet Office with No.10 Data Science and i.AI, DSIT including the Responsible Technology Adoption Unit), arm's length and public bodies (including ICO, GIAA, NHS, ONS, Scottish Government), industry (Amazon (AWS), Google, IBM, Microsoft) and academic institutes (including the Alan Turing Institute).
Date: February 2025
What it is: Non-statutory UK government guidance that updates and replaces the Generative AI Framework for HMG (January 2024) and widens it to all forms of AI. It sets 10 principles for AI use in government and public sector organisations, then gives guidance on understanding AI, building AI solutions (team, skills, user research, use cases, support structures), buying AI (business cases, procurement guidance, routes to market, CCS agreements), and using AI safely and responsibly (ethics, legal considerations, data protection and privacy, security, governance, risk, quality assurance). An appendix gives six public-sector case studies.
What it is for: To help 'government departments and public sector organisations harness the power of a wider range of AI technologies safely, effectively, and responsibly' (Foreword); a consistent approach for the UK government to use AI tools, to be used alongside each organisation's own policies (Principle 10).
Other important notes: Binding status: guidance; it uses 'must', 'should', 'need to' and 'consider' but states no sanctions for its own requirements. Many 'must' statements restate other instruments: law (UK GDPR, Data Protection Act 2018, Equality Act 2010 and the Public Sector Equality Duty, human rights, Public Contract Regulations 2015, Procurement Act 2023) or other policy (Secure by Design principles, government Service Standard, ATRS for central government departments and in-scope arm's length bodies, spend controls, Green Book above about £10 million, DDaT Playbook on a comply-or-explain basis). Addressees: written to 'you', meaning government departments, public sector organisations and their staff and teams; some passages name specific holders (end-users, SROs, decision makers, data controllers, organisers of meetings, commercial teams, cybersecurity teams, vendors). Coding approach: the Principles section is coded where it holds points not stated more fully in the body. 'Practical recommendations' boxes are coded only where the body text lacks the point; such entries are marked in the note. Appendix case studies are not coded, since the document says they 'should not be treated as formal advice'. Security scenarios are coded only where a recommendation is stated generally. The 'Adversaries using AI' passages and the meeting-transcription rule are edge cases (AI used by others against the body) and are marked in notes. Inconsistency: ATRS scope is stated as 'All central government departments and certain arm’s length bodies' (Transparency section) but 'all government departments and certain arm’s length bodies' (AI systems inventory). The text has no page numbers, so locations are section headings. Extraction problems: some sentences are truncated or lost, e.g. 'seek support from data ethics, project.' (Using AI safely and responsibly intro); 'and minimise the risk of' (Data protection and privacy); 'Refer to the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO)'s guidance on Unit (RTA)’s PET adoption guide' (Public AI APIs); a fragment 'sensitive information.' in the NHS user research finder case study; the end matter is partly missing. The source also names DSIT as 'Department for Science, Information and Technology' in places and cites 'Article 35(3)(a)' for three DPIA triggers. Bearing on checking AI outputs: the document asks for testing before deployment and regular checks of live tools; quantitative testing and validation on every update under change control; objective measures and accuracy measures; measurements of output accuracy and quality across protected characteristics; bias review by group including intersectional groups; testing outputs against known good responses and against existing knowledge; human validation of high-risk outputs; end-user checks that outputs are accurate, non-discriminatory, non-harmful and lawful; human review before automated actions; code review of LLM-generated code; ongoing performance monitoring for drift, bias and hallucination. The metrics and thresholds are mostly not specified.

Title: AI Watch. Road to the Adoption of Artificial Intelligence by the Public Sector: A Handbook for Policymakers, Public Administrations and Relevant Stakeholders (EUR 31054 EN)
Who wrote it: Manzoni M. (European Commission, JRC), Medaglia R. (Copenhagen Business School), Tangi L. (European Commission, JRC), Van Noordt C. (Tallinn University of Technology), Vaccari L. (independent researcher) and Gattwinkel D. (European Commission, DG CONNECT). Published by the Joint Research Centre as a JRC Science for Policy report, produced under AI Watch, which the JRC and DG CONNECT run jointly.
Date: 2022 (the national strategies table was last updated in November 2021; the survey ran from March to July 2021)
What it is: A JRC Science for Policy handbook. It sets out 16 recommendations in four areas of intervention, each broken down into actions: (1) value-oriented, human-centric and trustworthy AI; (2) coordinated governance, convergence of regulations and capacity building; (3) a shared AI digital ecosystem; (4) sustainability and impact assessment. It also gives a state of play (benefits, risks, barriers, EU policies, national strategies). Annexes: (1) a mapping of actions to five stakeholder groups (EU institutions and international authorities; central public authorities; decentralised public administrations; civil society and user representatives; R&D institutions and academia), marked as leading or contributing; (2) supporting sources; (3) a table of national AI strategies; (4) findings from a survey of 58 public-sector practitioners.
What it is for: To give policymakers, public administrations and other stakeholders at EU, national, regional and local levels recommendations and actions that promote the adoption of 'safe, lawful, inclusive and trustworthy AI' by public sector administrations in the EU. It is offered in support of the Coordinated Plan on AI 2021 Review and as feedback for future revisions of national strategies.
Other important notes: Not binding. The legal notice says 'The scientific output expressed does not imply a policy position of the European Commission'. Section 1.3 says the handbook's purpose 'is not to regulate specific aspects of AI, but rather to provide hands-on guidance'. Most actions are worded as 'could be considered', 'suggested' or 'recommended'. Holders are rarely named: most actions are passive. Annex 1 assigns leading and contributing stakeholder groups only by dark and light grey shading, which the text extraction does not keep, so holders cannot be recovered from Annex 1. Where the body names no holder, the coding says 'not stated'. Annex 1 sometimes words actions differently from the body text (for example 'should' rather than 'could' for national observatories), and it numbers Recommendation 3.3 as a second '3.2'. The body text was coded. Most of the handbook promotes adoption: funding, GovTech, data spaces, research networks and digital twins. Comparatively little concerns assurance or accountability for individual tools. Adoption-only items are coded with a '[scope doubt]' flag rather than dropped. The handbook uses the definition of an AI system from the 2021 AI Act proposal and describes that Act as 'currently under discussion', so it predates the adopted AI Act. Figures 1 and 2 and the Annex 4 survey charts are images and do not appear in the text. The text was extracted with pypdf and contains spacing errors such as 'governm ent' and 'th e', which the quotes keep. The handbook names no checks on AI outputs beyond pointing to ALTAI self-assessment, regulatory sandboxes, common testing criteria and impact assessment frameworks, and it specifies no metrics.

Title: Auditing AI Systems: A guide for public auditors (auditingalgorithms.net, with Audit Helper Tool), introduced by the NAO page 'AI auditing tool'
Who wrote it: The Supreme Audit Institutions of Brazil, Finland, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway and the UK (the UK SAI is the National Audit Office). The website is maintained by NAO Norway (Riksrevisjonen). The introductory page is by the UK National Audit Office, which says it 'co-produced' the catalogue and helper tool.
Date: Guide dated 19 December 2025 (footnotes: 'Last update: December 2025'); NAO page dated 25 Feb 2026; both downloaded 28 October 2026.
What it is: A non-statutory joint audit guide for SAIs. It covers sources of audit criteria (EU AI Act, UK, Brazil, international standards, adjacent fields), audit depth, and an audit catalogue in six lifecycle areas (governance, data, model development, pre-deployment evaluation, deployment and change management, production). Each area gives 'Risks to consider' and 'Expected controls'. There are five appendices and an Excel Audit Helper Tool, which was not extracted.
What it is for: To help SAIs and individual auditors audit AI systems used by government agencies. The NAO page also presents it as helping public bodies understand AI-specific risks, 'build assurance into delivery, rather than bolting it on later' and 'avoid surprises at audit'.
Other important notes: Not binding. The guide says it 'is not a prescriptive set of criteria and should be used as a guide for developing or adapting auditing methodologies'. Expected controls are what auditors should expect auditee organisations to have; most are verbless list items or passive, so the holder is usually 'not stated' (nearest: the auditee organisation). The guide is international, not UK-specific. The descriptions of the EU AI Act, the UK framework (e.g. ATRS 'now mandatory for central government departments') and Brazil's TCU rules were treated as reports of other instruments and were not coded; only pointers that tell auditors to use a source were coded, as Resources mentions. Appendix 5 role descriptions are descriptive ('not exhaustive'). Only the governance-relevant roles were coded; purely technical roles (AI architect, data analyst, data engineer, developer, subject matter expert) were not. Navigation menus repeated on every page were ignored. Points that bear on checking AI outputs: verifying outputs against trusted sources; output consistency tested by running the same prompt multiple times; human-in-the-loop validation; LLM-as-a-judge to be 'sufficiently evaluated by the project owner'; and auditors testing outputs directly when they have access. The guide also says AI tools were used to prepare visuals and consolidate the guide and helper tool, 'with thorough verification by the authors' (practice; not coded). UK268 entries are split across UK268__a1.jsonl, UK268__a2.jsonl and UK268__a3.jsonl because of their length.

Title: Artificial Intelligence Security Policy (DWP)
Who wrote it: Department for Work and Pensions (DWP). The accountable owner is the DWP Chief Security Officer, acting through the Deputy Director for Security Policy and Central Services / the Security and Data Protection directorate.
Date: Updated 6 May 2026 (GOV.UK page printed 11/05/2026).
What it is: A departmental security policy, one of the DWP security policies and standards published on GOV.UK under DWP procurement. It has policy statements, accountabilities, compliance clauses, Annex A (Third Party Artificial Intelligence security policy for suppliers) and Annex B (governance boards and associated teams).
What it is for: To set end-user responsibilities for using AI tools on official DWP business: acceptable use, approval for sensitive data, checking the accuracy of AI output, transparency (ATRS, declaring use), data protection and incident reporting. It sets parallel requirements for suppliers and their third parties.
Other important notes: Mandatory for DWP employees and contractors using DWP equipment or licensed software ('users') and for suppliers who meet the Annex A criteria. It covers 'All AI tools', including generative AI, machine learning and LLMs. The policy's terms table defines its verbs: must = mandatory, should = advisory, may = approval, can = capability or possibility. It says it 'does not replace legal or regulatory requirements'; no statute is cited as its basis apart from the Equality Act 2010 reference in statement 5. Consequences: line managers act on non-compliance under the DWP Discipline Policy, and failure to report a security incident 'could result in disciplinary action and ... dismissal'. On checking AI outputs: statement 10 (users) and Annex A statement 4 (suppliers) require checking the 'accuracy, reliability, and credibility of AI output' for misinformation or bias 'to the best of their ability'; no method, comparator or metric is given. Two approval bodies are named (the Digital Design Authority for new tools and use cases; the AI Delivery Board for formal sign-off of AI implementation), and their relationship is not stated. The text was extracted from a PDF print of the GOV.UK page, so hyperlink URLs are truncated to '(' lines. Quotes keep the extraction's line breaks as \n. The Annex A accountabilities block has no heading in the extraction.

Title: Artificial intelligence in public services; Artificial intelligence: checklist for public bodies in England (EHRC guidance)
Who wrote it: Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC).
Date: Both pages published 1 September 2022, last updated 1 September 2022; held copies printed/extracted 28 October 2026.
What it is: Two web pages from a three-page EHRC guide. The first is an overview of AI in public services, covering its benefits, its risks and UK government resources. The second is a checklist for public bodies in England (and non-devolved and cross-border public bodies): ten suggested steps, followed by sections on thinking about equality from the start, keeping records, considering each protected characteristic, outsourced and bought AI, and ongoing monitoring.
What it is for: To help public bodies comply with the Public Sector Equality Duty (Equality Act 2010) when they procure, commission, build, adapt, use or oversee AI. The checklist is aimed especially at bodies in England, which have no specific duty to prepare or publish an equality impact assessment.
Other important notes: This is non-statutory regulator guidance on a statutory duty. It mixes statements of the duty ('must', 'need to'), recommendations ('should', 'We recommend') and optional steps ('you may want to take the following steps'; 'You should develop a checklist to fit your own circumstances'). The guide page covers England, Scotland and Wales; the checklist covers England and non-devolved and cross-border public bodies, so it is relevant to UK-level bodies. The guide says it does not cover breaches of other laws such as the Data Protection Act 2018 and the Human Rights Act 1998. The middle page of the guide, 'Artificial intelligence: meeting the Public Sector Equality Duty (PSED)', was not among the assigned files and was not coded. The police facial-recognition example (suspension pending review, then monitoring) and the linked 'Artificial intelligence case studies: Good practice by local authorities' were treated as practice and not coded. On checking AI outputs, the guide asks bodies to 'make sure AI is working as intended' and to monitor whether people with protected characteristics are 'treated more or less well than other people'; it gives no method, threshold or frequency beyond 'regular'. Quotes keep the PDF extraction's line breaks as \n. All eight cells have entries, so no empty-cell notes were needed.

Title: Commission Guidelines on the implementation of the transparency obligations for certain AI systems under Article 50 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the 'AI Act'), C(2026) 5054 final: Communication to the Commission approving the content of the draft, and its Annex (the guidelines)
Who wrote it: European Commission (Brussels).
Date: 20 July 2026 (C(2026) 5054 final). The communication says formal adoption will follow once all language versions exist, and that the guidelines apply only from then; formal adoption is not recorded in these files.
What it is: Non-binding Commission guidance issued under AI Act Art. 96(1)(d) interpreting the four Article 50 transparency obligations and the horizontal requirements of Art. 50(5): 50(1) providers of AI systems that interact directly with people must ensure people are told they are dealing with AI; 50(2) providers of generative systems must mark outputs in a machine-readable way and make them detectable, with effective, interoperable, robust and reliable solutions; 50(3) deployers of emotion recognition and biometric categorisation systems must inform exposed persons; 50(4) deployers must disclose deep fakes and AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, unless under human review or editorial control with editorial responsibility. It also covers who counts as provider or deployer, scope exclusions, exceptions (obviousness, law enforcement, standard editing, B2B/industrial), interplay with other EU law, codes of practice, enforcement (market surveillance authorities, AI Office, EDPS), penalties, and entry into application (2 August 2026; AI Omnibus transition to 2 December 2026 for Art. 50(2)). The annex is 50 numbered pages with 155 numbered paragraphs.
What it is for: To give competent authorities, providers and deployers practical guidance for consistent compliance with Article 50 from 2 August 2026.
Other important notes: Binding force: the guidelines are non-binding ('Any authoritative interpretation of the AI Act may ultimately only be given by the Court of Justice'), but the duties they interpret are statutory duties under the AI Act. Public-sector relevance: providers and deployers are defined to include 'public authorities, agencies or other bodies'; the document's own examples include a public authority's in-house chatbot, public-service chatbots and helpdesks, police chatbots and hotlines, fraud-reporting portals run by public authorities, a meteorological institute's AI-generated warning, and public safety warnings approved by a public official. EU institutions, bodies and agencies face fines up to EUR 750 000, with the EDPS as their market surveillance authority. Points bearing on checking AI outputs: human review for the Art. 50(4) text exception must be a deliberate substantive examination including fact-checking, and AI changes after sign-off void the exception; 'AI-generated summaries of text' require marking while translations and transcriptions do not; internal employee-facing assistants for AI-literate trained staff can fall under the obviousness exception; organisation-internal texts are not 'published'. Coding choices by this coder: Art. 50 disclosure duties are coded both as Delivery/Design (the holder implements them) and Accountability/Design (disclosure to the people concerned, enforced with fines); scope and exception passages are coded as Decision-making/Design; interplay paragraphs that only restate other EU law (consumer, data protection, DSA, media, IP) were mostly not coded, as reports of other instruments. Output is split across EU_Art50__a1.jsonl to EU_Art50__a5.jsonl. Text extracted with pypdf; extraction errors (e.g. 'c ompliance', 'lifecy cle', 'certa in') are kept in quotes, and line breaks inside quotes are joined with a single space.

Title: Artificial Intelligence - A governance framework (Note for the attention of the Members of the Bureau, D(2024)6679, PE 755.624/BUR)
Who wrote it: European Parliament, the Secretary-General; addressed to the Members of the Bureau.
Date: 5 March 2024 (stamped '- 5 MARS 2024')
What it is: A five-page note asking the Bureau to approve a governance framework for AI in the Parliament. It sets out strategic orientations (scope, governance, compliance and control) and proposes a structure: a Governance Board (Chair appointed by the Secretary-General), an AI Competence Centre in the ICT services, an AI roadmap, and an Inter-DG network of AI business partners, plus risk and impact assessment within a validation process, with suspension for non-compliance.
What it is for: To let the Parliament's administration develop AI capability 'in a sustainable and ethically responsible manner', building on the 2020 guidelines (EP2020), with a validation process for AI projects, end-user engagement, and room to integrate EU legislation such as the AI Act.
Other important notes: Non-statutory internal governance of the European Parliament; applies to AI used to support Members and the administration, including tools developed in-house or acquired. Status: a proposal; the WG ICT endorsed it on 22 February 2024 (as the note reports), but Bureau approval is not recorded in this text and a redacted block follows the decision paragraph. Main checks: risk and impact assessment in validation (transparency, cybersecurity, organisational impact, upskilling/reskilling), regular safety and risk assessment in the roadmap, continuous oversight; no metrics or intervals stated. One sanction: non-compliance with the assessment process should lead to suspension of the project (who decides is not stated). One reporting line: Governance Board Chair to WG ICT. AI tools not offered by Parliament are referred to the cyber security and cyber defence framework. The source is a transcription of a scanned PDF made by Claude Code on 29 October 2026, keeping original typing errors (e.g. 'chabots'); the transcription note says quotes should be checked against the page images before citing.

Title: Guidelines for the responsible use of Artificial Intelligence in the European Parliament (PE 650.282/BUR/GT, D(2020) 15247)
Who wrote it: European Parliament, Directorate-General for Innovation and Technological Support (DG ITEC), the Director-General (acting); addressed to the Members of the Bureau Working Party on ICT Innovation Strategy.
Date: 2020 (no day or month on the note itself; the file name and reference give 2020)
What it is: A seven-page internal note asking the Bureau Working Party to endorse guidelines on the responsible use of AI in the Parliament. It defines AI, describes three domains (assisted, augmented, autonomous intelligence), sets out compliance and transparency expectations, a four-phase project lifecycle, five lifecycle questions, and four principles (ethical and lawful; safe and robust; secure and privacy compliant; transparent and explainable), each with a rationale and a list of requirements.
What it is for: To give direction for the Parliament's first uses of AI to improve or create services for Members and the administration, focusing on legal and ethical risks, and to lead to an AI strategy for the Parliament in 2021.
Other important notes: Non-statutory, internal to the European Parliament; applies to the Parliament's own AI initiatives (Members, staff, administration). Endorsement is requested but not recorded in this text. Most requirements are imperatives with no named holder; the nearest named actor is Parliament's administration. No decision-maker for individual tools, no approval gate, no reporting line, audit, complaint route or sanction is stated. Checks named: representative datasets, bias-detection control mechanisms, adversarial testing, corner-case coverage, data-origin traceability; none has a trigger beyond 'all stages of the lifecycle' or a metric. Footnote 1 says the Information Security policy cited is pending approval. Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 is the only legislation named. The source text was extracted from a PDF with pypdf; some words are split by extraction (e.g. 'require s', 'pre -condition'), kept as in the text.

Title: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 8 July 2026 amending Regulations (EU) 2024/1689, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2023/1230 as regards the simplification of the implementation of harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Digital Omnibus on AI)
Who wrote it: European Parliament and Council of the European Union (ordinary legislative procedure, on a Commission proposal); signed by R. Metsola (EP President) and T. Byrne (Council President); published in the Official Journal, L series, 24 July 2026 (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj)
Date: Adopted 8 July 2026; published 24 July 2026; in force on the third day after publication (Art. 4). Several amendments apply from 27 July 2026; new Art. 5 prohibitions from 2 December 2026; high-risk Chapter III Sections 1-3 from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) and 2 August 2028 (Annex I).
What it is: An EU amending regulation (47 recitals, 4 articles, new Annex XIV to the AI Act). Article 1 amends the AI Act (Reg. 2024/1689) in 43 points; Article 2 amends the civil aviation regulation (Reg. 2018/1139); Article 3 amends the Machinery Regulation (Reg. 2023/1230).
What it is for: To simplify and ease implementation of the AI Act: delays high-risk obligations; softens AI literacy to a duty to 'take measures to support'; creates a stand-alone legal basis (Art. 4a) for processing special-category data for bias detection, extended to deployers; adds prohibitions on AI generating non-consensual intimate material and child sexual abuse material; extends SME relief to small mid-caps; centralises supervision of GPAI-based AI systems and VLOP/VLOSE-integrated systems in the AI Office with new investigation, fining and publication powers (Art. 75-75d); strengthens fundamental-rights bodies' access to information (Art. 77); adds templates and guidance duties (FRIA questionnaire, post-market monitoring plan, simplified technical documentation); restructures sandboxes and real-world testing (incl. a new EDPS sandbox for EU institutions and Art. 60a); moves machinery to a sectoral approach.
Other important notes: Binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States (Art. 4). Title: Guidance for Risk Management of Artificial Intelligence systems

What it is for: To help EUIs acting as controllers under Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 (EUDPR) identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, mainly through technical measures. Extraction: pypdf text; some words split ('r obustness', 'un der', 'e nsure'), some double spaces kept in quotes; Figures 1-3 and the Annex 2 diagram not fully captured; Annex tables flattened. Output split over EDPS_AI_risk__a1.jsonl to __a5.jsonl because of output length limits.

Coder's note, not stated in the document (checker to confirm against the GDPR): under GDPR Art. 6(1), last subparagraph, public authorities cannot rely on legitimate interest for processing in the performance of their tasks, so section 3.3 bears mainly on developers and providers of models that public bodies later use, not on public bodies' own task processing. Mentions the AI Act declaration of conformity (para 131). Extraction artefacts: split words (e.g. 'controlle rs', 'approp riate') and inline footnote numbers; quotes reproduce them exactly.

Title: Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content
Who wrote it: Drafted in two working groups whose chairs are named on the cover. Working Group 1 (Section 1): Chair Kalina Bontcheva; Vice-Chairs Dino Pedreschi and Christian Riess. Working Group 2 (Section 2): Chair Anja Bechmann; Vice-Chairs Giovanni De Gregorio and Madalina Botan. Annex 1 says the EU icons were developed by the AI Office. The text does not say who adopted or approved the Code. Source URL is a European Commission newsroom (DG CONNECT) link.
Date: 10 June 2026 (per the assignment and file name; no date appears in the extracted text)
What it is: A voluntary code of practice under the EU AI Act for the Article 50 transparency obligations. Section 1 covers marking and detection of AI-generated or manipulated content by providers of generative AI systems (Art. 50(2) and (5)). Section 2 covers labelling of deep fakes, and of AI-generated or manipulated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, by deployers (Art. 50(4) and (5)). Annex 1 contains the EU icons. Each section has objectives, recitals, commitments and measures, and Section 1 has a glossary.
What it is for: To serve as a guiding document for showing compliance with Art. 50(2), (4) and (5), and to let competent market surveillance authorities assess consistently, across the Union, the compliance of Signatories who rely on it. Adherence 'does not constitute conclusive evidence of compliance'.
Other important notes: Binding only on Signatories who adhere. Within the Code, 'will' marks mandatory measures that Signatories must meet to comply and that MSAs monitor; 'encouraged' marks optional but recommended measures; 'may' marks optional measures or flexibility. The Code states no sanctions. It is not aimed at the public sector. Public bodies are covered as deployers, for example when publishing AI-generated text that informs the public on matters of public interest, or deep fakes (there is a placement variant for closed internal professional contexts such as staff training). They may also be covered as providers if they put generative AI systems into service [inference]. Section 2 Commitment 4 (human review and a named person with editorial responsibility before publication) is the route out of labelling for AI-drafted public text [inference from the Art. 50(4) text and the commitment's heading]. EDGE CASE: Section 1 gives competent authorities, regulators and law enforcement free, unlimited access to detection tools for checking whether incoming content is AI-generated; that is AI used by others, not by the body. The reproduced Art. 50(4) legal text exempts uses authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences. Value chain: model providers and third-party marking and detection providers may adhere voluntarily; relying on them does not shift the Signatory's responsibility. Bears on checking AI outputs: Commitment 3 and Measure 4.2 set quality requirements and testing for marking and detection (error rates on held-out data, robustness to everyday alterations and adversarial attacks, user-based effectiveness assessment, testing before market placement and regularly after). Interoperability deadline: 2 February 2027. Prospective roles not yet recorded: AI Office endorsement of benchmarks, an EU repository, and the taskforce. I coded the 'LEGAL TEXT' boxes reproducing Art. 50 as reports of another instrument and cite them only in notes. Extraction: cover and section-title pages are mostly blank lines, the icon figures are absent, and there are split words (e.g. 'capitali sed', '202 7').

Title: Commission Guidelines on the scope of the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models established by Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act)
Who wrote it: European Commission (Communication from the Commission, C(2025) 7719 final). Implementation of Chapter V is entrusted to the AI Office. Who wrote it: Ofgem (Office of Gas and Electricity Markets), Emerging Technologies Team; foreword by Tim Jarvis, Interim Chief Executive. Contact: Jonathan Thurlwell.
Date: Published 13 May 2026 (second edition; first edition May 2025)
What it is: Sector regulator guidance setting out good practice for the ethical adoption of AI in Great Britain's energy sector, organised around four outcomes (safety, security, fairness, environmental sustainability) and three areas (governance and policies, risk, competencies), with sector case examples and six appendices (legal and regulatory obligations; AI standards; supply chain; data; cyber security; transparency and explainability). Version 2 adds a transparency and explainability good practice and appendix.
What it is for: To encourage an ethical, proportionate, outcomes-focused approach to AI adoption by energy sector stakeholders, complementing (not replacing) existing licence conditions, codes and legislation, and to tell regulated persons how existing enforcement powers apply where AI use breaches their obligations.
Other important notes: Binding status: the guidance itself is good practice and non-binding ('This guidance complements, and does not replace, existing legal and regulatory obligations'; it 'does not constitute legal advice'). Appendix 1 restates binding obligations (licence conditions, Competition Act 1998, REMIT, NIS Regulations 2018, UK GDPR) and Ofgem's enforcement powers (penalties up to 10% of turnover; director disqualification), and states that AI use does not excuse or mitigate a breach. Audience (1.12): 'all stakeholders involved with AI in the sector', including licensees, market participants, operators of essential services, technology companies, AI developers, consumer groups, other regulators and government. Scope doubt: most holders are private regulated energy companies; public-sector relevance rests on energy as a regulated public service and critical infrastructure and on government and regulators being in the stated audience; Ofgem is an independent statutory regulator. Much of the text is worded as good practice in the present tense ('Stakeholders implement ...'), and section 6 case-example 'considerations' are described as good practice actions, not exhaustive; I coded these as design and noted the wording. Some normative statements sit under 'Case example' headings (3.10-3.12); coded as design with a flag. Checking AI outputs: testing before use (4.13), validation against known good data, research or expertise for black-box AI including LLM hallucinations (6.24-6.25), drift monitoring (4.12, A4.4f), human oversight (4.16), and records explaining the basis of AI decisions (3.13c); metrics are suggested but not specified. Mentions non-state resources (Microsoft Responsible AI Standard v2, University of York AMLAS, ISO/IEC, NIST). The glossary (pp.27-32) and background chronology (1.20) were not coded. Statements that only remind readers of other legislation (1.13, A1.5, A1.11) were treated as reports and not coded separately.

Title: AI Testing and Assurance Framework for Public Sector
Who wrote it: Cross-Government Testing Community (UK). Author: Mibin Boban, xGov Testing Community Chair / Head of Quality Engineering, GDS (5 June 2025). Working-group and review comments from Home Office, GDS, DWP, DfE, NHS England, National Highways (DfT), DSIT, MHRA and 2i Testing (a private firm), June-August 2025.
Date: 2025 (review log dated 5 June to 27 August 2025; page marked 'Live')
What it is: A cross-government framework for testing, evaluation and assurance of AI systems in the public sector, covering rule-based, machine learning, generative and agentic AI. It sets out 21 quality attributes in four themes, eleven testing and evaluation principles, a seven-phase 'continuous defensive assurance' lifecycle model, nine testing modules (each with core practices, approaches by AI type, example tests, example metrics, evidence artefacts and pitfalls), and pointers to tools.
What it is for: To give 'a shared reference point for government teams who are responsible for testing, evaluation and the wider assurance of AI systems' and to 'establish a minimum baseline of testing and evaluation for AI systems that impact the public', for use across UK Government departments, agencies and other public sector bodies developing or procuring AI.
Other important notes: Binding status: non-statutory and explicitly not mandatory ('this is not a checklist or a rigid standard'; 'a common foundation, not a fixed prescription'); departments 'can adopt, adapt, or extend' it. Some passages still use 'must' (e.g. monitoring after deployment, change sign-off, residual risks 'must be formally acknowledged'); I recorded these as 'must (in a non-mandatory framework)'. It names no sanctions and no body that checks compliance. Example metrics and thresholds (e.g. PSI ≤ 0.2, demographic parity gap ≤ 10%, > 80% of generative outputs rated acceptable by human reviewers) are offered as examples, not requirements; I put them in notes rather than coding them as separate entries. Highly relevant to checking AI outputs: human evaluation of generative outputs, counterfactual prompt testing for bias, jailbreak and falsehood testing, prompt-log traceability, comparing real-world outcomes against predictions, override and kill-switch capability, and the risk that staff who validate AI outputs lose skills. Accountability content is thin: go/no-go and sign-off by SROs, governance boards and ethics panels; ATRS publication appears only as an example checklist item; external audit 'possibly' for high-risk AI; storing output logs for FOI, audits or investigations. Mentions a private provider (OpenAI) only as a pricing example. The text was extracted from a web page (markdown); link targets are lost (e.g. '[Service Standard](' ), and I quoted these as they appear. Statements cite the Equality Act 2010, GDPR, Data Protection Act, Public Sector Bodies Accessibility Regulations and WCAG 2.2 AA as things testing supports, not as the source of the framework's own requirements.

Title: The NAO's AI Strategy: The future of Artificial Intelligence in our work
Who wrote it: National Audit Office (NAO), UK; corporate document (© National Audit Office 2026). No named author.
Date: 2026 (assignment gives August 2026; the text itself shows only the 2026 copyright year)
What it is: The NAO's corporate AI strategy: a definition of AI, seven AI principles for the NAO's own use, a vision, three goals (Trust, Value, Impact) with success measures, two maturity pathways (assuring AI in government; the NAO's own use of AI) from L0 'Foundations' (2025) to L4 (2035 and beyond), a section on auditing AI in government, workforce plans, a roadmap of priority actions in five areas for 2026-27 to 2028-29 and beyond, a governance section naming the Executive Team, NAO Board, AI Governance Board and service lines, and plans for engaging government, other supreme audit institutions, audit firms, ICAEW and the FRC.
What it is for: To set out how the NAO will (a) audit and give independent assurance over AI used by the public bodies it audits, reporting to Parliament, and (b) adopt and govern AI responsibly in its own audit and corporate work.
Other important notes: Binding status: an organisational strategy; commitments are self-imposed ('we will'), non-statutory as written, with no sanctions or consequences stated. It covers two objects: the NAO's own AI tools (the NAO is itself a public body using AI) and the AI of audited bodies, which the NAO commits to audit; I coded the audit commitments as Accountability with the NAO as holder and Parliament as the body it reports to (vision, p.5). The NAO's statutory audit powers are not cited. The roadmap table (pp.14-15) has year columns (2026-27, 2027-28, 2028-29 and beyond) that the text extraction does not preserve, so the timing of each action cannot be read from the text; extraction also joins some words ('toidentify', 'reflectuse', 'governanceis', 'Parliament,regulators'), quoted as they appear. Checking AI outputs: principles call for 'validation, testing and human oversight to ensure outputs are fit for purpose' and for outputs that 'can be understood, tested and challenged'; the roadmap commits to developing staff skills 'for critically reviewing AI-assisted outputs'; no metrics, triggers or comparators are given. Some content is about AI used by others to read NAO outputs (AI-mediated access to NAO insight); flagged as an edge case. The goals' success measures (pp.6) concern the strategy's own performance and were not coded separately. Copilot is named as a tool to roll out, without its supplier.

Title: AI Insights (GDS series), 15 chapters coded as one document: Introduction; Agentic AI; Agentic RAG; Agentic Workflow; AI Coding Assistants for developers in HMG; Generative AI; Integrated Agents; Large language models (LLMs) Bias; Model Distillation; Prompt Engineering; Prompt Risks; RAG Systems; Synthetic Data; Using AI to manage shared drives; Using AI to manage the digital heap
Who wrote it: Government Digital Service (GDS), per the Introduction ('a new collection of articles published by the Government Digital Service (GDS)', 'written by government technologists and subject matter experts'). Each extracted page header lists 'Department for Digital, Culture, Media & Sport' and 'Government Digital Service'. The Integrated Agents chapter speaks 'As the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology' (line 75). The AI Coding Assistants chapter says it was 'developed in collaboration with senior stakeholders, technologists, and assurance teams'. The two records-management chapters are written 'from a knowledge and information management (KIM) perspective'. The header department name and the DSIT voice are recorded as the text gives them; this coder has not checked which department currently hosts GDS.
Date: Every chapter is marked 'Updated 3 August 2026'. First-publication dates are not given in the extracted text. Downloaded 28 October 2026 from gov.uk/government/publications/ai-insights.
What it is: A GOV.UK publication of type 'Guidance': a series of articles that 'complements the AI Playbook and its training resources by focusing on AI topics that were not discussed in the playbook' (Introduction). The chapters range from technical explainers (RAG, distillation, prompt engineering, synthetic data) to practical guidance with explicit requirements (AI coding assistants structured on the 10 AI Playbook principles; LLM bias with a three-step risk matrix; integrated agent entities; using AI to review shared drives and the 'digital heap').
What it is for: To 'help government departments and public sector organisations implement and use artificial intelligence (AI) solutions effectively, safely and securely', to clarify AI/ML terminology for the public sector, and to give practical implementation advice (Introduction). Readers are told to use it 'alongside the guidance in the Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government and your organisation’s policies, ensuring that you have the right assurance in place'.
Other important notes: (1) Binding force: the series never says it is mandatory and names no enforcement. It often uses 'must' and once says testing 'should be mandatory' and profiling is 'mandatory prior to any model change', but no consequence for non-compliance is stated. Entries record the verb as 'guidance: must (binding force not stated)'. (2) Audience: the Introduction names government departments and public sector organisations. The AI Coding Assistants chapter is aimed at HMG developers and senior leaders but says it 'can be used by individuals and organisations in both the public and the private sector'. The two KIM chapters are aimed at government KIM professionals. Many technical chapters speak as 'we' without naming a holder; those entries record holder 'not stated' and the series audience as the nearest actor. (3) Where the requirements are densest: the LLM Bias chapter has a risk matrix whose required mitigations and evaluations rise by risk level. At Critical these include 'Mandatory human approval decisions', 'User appeal mechanism', 'Complete audit trail', 'Monthly external audit' and 'Auto-rollback on threshold breach'. Step 1 defines only low, medium and high, so the route to Critical is by inference from the one-step escalation rule. The Integrated Agents chapter sets an approval gate (written approval from 'a manager or responsible officer' before deployment), an internal inventory and audits for user-built agent entities. The digital-heap chapter sets benchmarks before development, evaluation before use (sample 10% or 1,000 records), audit trails for AI-based disposition, and the rule that the KIM team decides when an AI model is accurate enough to rely on. The shared-drives chapter sets a departmental approval process before AI-informed disposition decisions are actioned, and points to the algorithmic transparency recording standard for publication without saying whether publication is mandatory. (4) Not coded (by rule or as out of scope): statements that only report other instruments (Public Records Act 20-year transfer rule, Code of Practice on the Management of Records, FOI Act exemptions, Government Cloud First policy, Service Standard/TCoP as such, DSIT's AI implementation phases guide); case studies treated as practice (Cabinet Office automated document review and its published ATRS return; FCDO Services digital sensitivity review; DESNZ SharePoint provisioning; Microsoft Syntex/Copilot experimentation); records-management steps with no AI element (read-only drives, migration steps, retention bands as such); pure engineering and architecture advice (composition and interfaces, modular architecture, chunking, student-model sizing); and technical descriptions. (5) Companion Insights cited but not in the 15 chapters (LLM Testing, Evaluation Metrics, LLM Safeguarding) were not available to code. (6) Edge case: the Prompt Risks chapter is about attacks on the body's own AI systems (prompt injection, jailbreaking, data/RAG poisoning, denial of wallet). It names 'generative phishing' as a vulnerability, which would be AI used by others against the body, but only in passing; not coded. (7) Value chain: suppliers and model providers are named often (GitHub, OpenAI, Microsoft, Google, AWS, IBM, HuggingFace, vendors of integrated tools), but the series puts no duties on them. Their indemnities, terms, account managers, training credits and vulnerability updates are coded as mentioned resources. Duties fall on the deploying organisation (e.g. 'Such tools will still need evaluation prior to use'). (8) Checking AI outputs: across the chapters the series asks for human review of outputs ('You’re responsible for checking and controlling their output'; peer review of AI-assisted code before merging; human-in-the-loop wherever decisions are ones 'your organisation would normally expect to account for'), recording of prompts and responses, validation 'against ground truth or expert judgement', sample checks, and retesting on any model change. (9) Locations give the chapter title, section heading and line numbers in the extracted .txt files (no page numbers exist). (10) Extraction quirks preserved in quotes: 'Use Ai', 'Chekov', a double space in 'Only use  integrated'.

Title: Introduction to AI assurance
Who wrote it: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT); ministerial foreword by Viscount Camrose, Minister for Artificial Intelligence and Intellectual Property. Back page: 'Introduction to AI Assurance v1.1, Designed by magnetic'.
Date: February 2024
What it is: A 44-page introductory guidance document on AI assurance: concepts (trust, justified trust), the AI assurance toolkit (risk and impact assessment, bias and compliance audit, conformity assessment, formal verification), the role of technical standards, the assurance ecosystem and its stakeholders, illustrative case studies, and five key actions for organisations. Described as 'the first in a series of guidance' and 'a living, breathing document'.
What it is for: To help organisations (industry and regulators) understand AI assurance and how to operationalise the five cross-cutting principles of the 2023 AI regulation white paper; to help organisations upskill and build assurance capability.
Other important notes: Non-binding guidance. Addressed to organisations in general (developers, procurers and deployers; SMEs; regulators), not specifically to the public sector, though the foreword mentions public services and one example (Ada Lovelace Institute AIA) concerns algorithms using public sector data. 'You' means the reader organisation. The only 'must' statements restate existing law (UK GDPR, Data Protection Act 2018, Equality Act 2010); the UKAS sourcing rule is stated as UK government policy. Not coded: the five principles (p.10) and the Bletchley Declaration (p.13), as reports of other instruments; the case studies (pp.33-38) and the landscape diagram (p.28), as illustrative practice; the 'Additional resources' list (p.43) beyond items already coded. Most resources are mentions of non-state providers rather than official offers; DSIT's own offers are the Portfolio of Assurance Techniques, the Fairness Innovation Challenge, the AI assurance team contact and planned sector guidance. For checking AI outputs: the document recommends performance testing against 'clear performance benchmarks', bias audits and formal verification, but sets no metrics, thresholds or triggers.

Title: AI Opportunities Action Plan
Who wrote it: Matt Clifford, commissioned by the Secretary of State for Science, Innovation and Technology (Peter Kyle MP, who wrote the foreword); published by DSIT as an 'Independent report' and 'Presented to Parliament by the Secretary of State Science, Innovation and Technology by Command of His Majesty' (CP1241).
Date: 13 January 2025
What it is: An independent report with 50 numbered recommendations in three sections: (1) foundations (compute, data, talent, regulation, safety and assurance); (2) adoption, including a 'Scan > Pilot > Scale' approach for AI in government and procurement; (3) 'homegrown AI' via a new UK Sovereign AI unit.
What it is for: To set out how the UK government can 'ramp up AI adoption across the UK to boost economic growth, provide jobs for the future and improve people's everyday lives', including government's role as 'a major user and customer of AI'.
Other important notes: Recommendations, not requirements: 'should' throughout, occasionally 'must'. This text does not record the government's acceptance of each recommendation (the foreword says 'Today, we have set out how we will rise to the challenge'). Nothing is statutory. Only parts concern AI tools used in the public sector: mainly 1.4 (regulators, AISI, assurance tools) and 2.2-2.3 (Scan > Pilot > Scale; procurement; shared infrastructure). Not coded as outside the object: most of 1.1-1.3 (compute for research, open data for developers, talent and visas), 2.4 (private-sector adoption: Industrial Strategy, AI Sector Champions), section 3 (UK Sovereign AI) and recommendation 44 (government APIs for external companies' tools; not AI used by public officials). Not coded as reports or practice: the 2.1 use-case examples (police 'automated threat and anomaly detection', NHS diagnostics, the Department for Education marking tool reported at '92% accuracy in a pilot'), the NHS AI Diagnostic Fund and AISI's past pre-deployment evaluations. For checking AI outputs: the plan calls for 'robust evaluation' of pilots, performance evaluations in contract terms and 'government-backed high-quality assurance tools that assess whether AI systems perform as claimed', but sets no metrics, thresholds or triggers. Its emphasis is speed and risk tolerance ('absorb some risk'; controls layered only 'as the investment-size gets larger').

Title: Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard Template V4 (Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard v4.0)
Who wrote it: The Algorithmic Transparency Team (ATRS team). The file header gives the issuer as Government Digital Service; the contact address is algorithmic-transparency@dsit.gov.uk.
Date: Not stated in the text (version 4.0). The 'All data' sheet is labelled 'Standard version v3.0'.
What it is: A spreadsheet template (extracted to text from the governance repo's preprocessed parquet, not from the original file) for a public body to complete an algorithmic transparency record. Sheets: Info; 0 Metadata; Tier 1 Summary (for the general public); Tier 2 sections 2.1 Owner and Responsibility, 2.2 Description and Rationale, 2.3 Deployment Context, 2.4.1 Tool, 2.4.2 Model (three copies), 2.4.3 Development Data, 2.4.4 Operational Data, 2.5 Risks, Mitigations and Impact Assessments; optional Dataset card and Extra space; plus back-end sheets (All data, Markdown, DSA table, Validation).
What it is for: To record information about an algorithmic tool used in the public sector, for review by the ATRS team and display in the ATRS repository of published records. Purpose given: 'increasing the visibility of algorithmic tools in the public sector'.
Other important notes: The template itself does not say who must complete a record or when; any mandate comes from elsewhere. Its fields are disclosure prompts: they ask whether and how the body does things (human review, performance evaluation, impact assessment, appeals) but do not require those things. I coded each field to the function it asks about, as Design, and noted 'disclosure only' where relevant. Many fields allow 'N/A'. The DSA table marks the fields 'required' TRUE. Unmodified off-the-shelf models (e.g. 'Web UI-based LLMs') may skip the Model and Development Data sections, so model performance need not be recorded for them. The 'All data' sheet (v3.0) has older wording that differs on substance in places (e.g. 'Describe any performance thresholds your model should exceed'; fairness subgroup analysis; maintenance by supplier or operator). I cite these in notes but did not code them as separate entries. Extraction and spreadsheet artefacts: '#REF!' errors in the DSA table; test content in the Markdown sheet ('Test tool', 'test@email.com'); a default 'East Midlands' value in field 0.4. Feedback spaces (on the ATRS itself, not the tool) are not coded. For checking AI outputs: the relevant fields are 2.3.2 (human review and how it is assured), 2.4.2.7 (model evaluation 'for readiness for deployment', with example metrics accuracy/precision/recall) and 2.4.1.4 (maintenance and review schedule).

Title: Implementing the UK’s AI Regulatory Principles: Initial Guidance for Regulators
Who wrote it: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT)
Date: February 2024
What it is: Phase one of three planned phases of non-statutory guidance for regulators. It sets out considerations ('could'), key questions and suggested technical standards for applying the five AI White Paper principles (safety, security and robustness; appropriate transparency and explainability; fairness; accountability and governance; contestability and redress) in regulators' tools and guidance. It also suggests how regulators can publish an update on their AI approach. Annex 1 lists existing AI guidance by UK regulators. Extracted from the governance repo's parquet (aies_subset), not directly from the PDF.
What it is for: To support regulators in interpreting and applying the principles within their remits and in developing tools and guidance for 'AI developers, deployers and end users', and to promote coherence across regulators. It also describes DSIT's new central function (risk analysis, coordination, a £10 million capability package).
Other important notes: Voluntary and non-binding: 'the principles are voluntary and how they are considered is ultimately at regulators’ discretion'; footnote 1 says the guidance is to be considered 'on a voluntary (non-statutory) basis'. Regulators with a 'technology agnostic' approach may treat parts as not applicable. Its direct addressees are regulators (inside the state). Duties on 'AI developers and deployers' reach them only through regulators' own tools and guidance. Public bodies are covered as 'AI deployers' ('Any individual or organisation that supplies or uses an AI application to provide a product or service to an end user') where they fall within a regulator's remit. The document notes that a regulator's ability to hold developers and deployers to account 'is also contingent on whether they are a regulated entity within that regulators’ remit', and that some regulators may only be able to place legal responsibility on deployers. Not coded: the boxed principle statements (restating the White Paper), the regulator collaboration example box and the White Paper background, as reports. Many 'key questions' are coded as 'good practice: question'; some are folded into the notes of related entries. For checking AI outputs: it suggests regular risk assessment and testing or due diligence along the supply chain, and notes that AI decisions 'may require more robust inspection than when decisions are made by humans'. It sets no metrics or thresholds and leaves definitions (safety, fairness) to each regulator. Extraction artefacts: 'action’s' and 'models2' (footnote marker) appear as in the source text.

Title: Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard - guidance for public sector bodies
Who wrote it: Government Digital Service (DSIT); GOV.UK guidance
Date: Updated 8 May 2025 (text is a GOV.UK print dated 09/05/2026)
What it is: Section-by-section guidance on what the ATRS is, who must use it, how to prepare (SPOC, lead, suppliers, what not to publish), how to complete each tier and section of the ATRS template, and how to submit, clear, publish, update and retire a record.
What it is for: To help public sector organisations complete and publish ATRS records describing the algorithmic tools they use and why, so as to support public understanding, SRO accountability, peer learning, fewer FOI requests and clarity for suppliers.
Other important notes: Mandatory by policy (not statute) for government departments and ALBs delivering public or frontline services or directly interacting with the public, for tools with significant influence on decisions with public effect or direct public interaction; recommended by the Data Standards Authority for the rest of the public sector. Most field instructions use 'should'; the one 'must' is completing the appeals field where UK GDPR Art. 22 applies. Publication is gated by the ATRS team requiring written confirmation of internal sign-off (team, SRO, comms). For unrefined off-the-shelf models (e.g. Web UI-based LLMs) the model and development-data sections are left blank. The record asks about bias evaluation and impact assessments but does not itself require them to be conducted. No sanction for non-compliance is stated. Companion to UK085 (scope and exemptions policy).

Title: Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS) Mandatory Scope and Exemptions Policy
Who wrote it: Government Digital Service (part of DSIT); GOV.UK policy paper
Date: Published 17 December 2024 (text is a GOV.UK print dated 11/05/2026)
What it is: A policy paper setting which organisations and which algorithmic tools are within the mandatory requirement to publish ATRS records, and how sensitive information may be exempted. Includes an annex of in-scope and out-of-scope example tools.
What it is for: To implement the February 2024 cross-government mandate (announced in the AI White Paper consultation response) that central government publish ATRS records, by drawing clear lines on organisational scope, tool scope (significant influence on decisions with public effect, or direct public interaction), lifecycle stage (Beta/Pilot or Production) and exemptions modelled on FOIA.
Other important notes: Mandatory by policy, not statute, for ministerial and non-ministerial departments and ALBs providing public or frontline services; recommended (DSA-endorsed) for the broader public sector. No sanction or compliance monitoring is stated. Exemption decisions are made by the publishing organisation using a hypothetical FOI test; no external approval of exemptions is stated. Annex 1 places ad-hoc internal LLM use (e.g. Copilot for meeting summaries) out of scope and LLM analysis of public submissions in scope. The text refers to commercial sensitivity as FOIA 'section 23' in 5.1 and 'Section 43' in 5.3 (inconsistency in the source). Companion to UK086 (ATRS guidance).

Title: Good practice guide for organisations using AI
Who wrote it: National Audit Office (NAO), the UK's independent public spending watchdog (Insight product, DP Ref 018501)
Date: May 2026
What it is: A non-binding good practice guide addressed to audit and risk assurance committees, setting out where AI is used in government, areas organisations need to consider (embedded AI, cloud services, productivity claims, external impacts of AI) and, for nine areas of focus (innovation, AI strategy, leadership and skills, data, security, pilots, scaling, guardrails, workforce and culture), commentary plus suggested questions committees could ask.
What it is for: To help audit and risk assurance committees oversee the planning, deployment and scaling of AI within public sector organisations, drawing on NAO findings, the government's AI Playbook and lessons from digital transformation.
Other important notes: Non-statutory and non-binding: its 'must' and 'should' statements are good practice, and most content is questions (coded as 'good practice: question'). It reports, without setting, several arrangements made elsewhere (DSIT and GDS roles, ATRS mandatory for central government, Secure by Design mandatory principles, Copilot as the main approved tool, ChatGPT Enterprise approved in some departments); these reports were not coded except where they state where responsibility sits. Contains an edge case: risks from AI used by others towards public bodies (surges in submissions, fraud, cyber-attacks). Names no sanctions and no specific accountable roles beyond audit committees and senior leaders. Says the guide 'will evolve as AI itself continues to evolve'.

Title: Guidelines for AI procurement
Who wrote it: Office for Artificial Intelligence (joint BEIS-DCMS unit), developed with the World Economic Forum Centre for the Fourth Industrial Revolution, GDS, Government Commercial Function and Crown Commercial Service
Date: Published June 2020 (text labelled 'Version 1.7X')
What it is: Guidance setting out ten guidelines for buying AI technology and AI-specific considerations at each procurement stage (preparation and planning, publication, selection/evaluation/award, contract implementation and ongoing management), with pointers to further reading and toolkits.
What it is for: To help central government departments (and optionally other public bodies) assess whether AI suits a problem and procure it effectively and ethically: data assessment, impact assessment, market engagement, explainability, avoiding vendor lock-in, evaluation of suppliers, liability allocation, knowledge transfer, ongoing model testing, auditability and end-of-life.
Other important notes: Non-statutory guidance; says it is 'not exhaustive' and assumes knowledge of procurement law (Public Contracts Regulations 2015 named as most relevant). Uses 'must' in places (oversight mechanisms, staff training, reporting of unauthorised behaviour, public benefit goals), but no sanction or enforcement is stated. Statutory references restated: Public Services (Social Value) Act 2012, Equality Act 2010 PSED, Data Protection legislation and GDPR. Places many duties on suppliers indirectly through tenders and contracts (data checks, team skills, knowledge transfer, liability). Mostly framed around machine learning; predates generative AI. The extracted text has column-break interleaving in several places (e.g. impact assessment review trigger, independent audits), noted in entries.

Title: The roadmap to an effective AI assurance ecosystem
Who wrote it: Centre for Data Ethics and Innovation (CDEI), with a ministerial foreword by Chris Philp MP; GOV.UK 'Independent report' (now under DSIT)
Date: Published 8 December 2021
What it is: A roadmap describing the vision for a UK AI assurance ecosystem, six priority areas (demand, market, standards, professionalisation, regulation, independent research), a summary table of current challenges and what needs to happen, and the CDEI's 2021/22 work programme.
What it is for: To shape and bring coherence to a nascent, economy-wide market of AI assurance tools and services (audits, impact assessments, certification), setting out roles different actors should play, as committed in the National AI Strategy.
Other important notes: Non-statutory and non-binding: most content is aspiration ('will need to', 'what needs to happen') or CDEI commitments to support, advise and convene. Economy-wide rather than public-sector specific; the only passage directly on public-sector AI is the CDEI commitment to embed assurance in partnership projects with defence-focused organisations, police forces and local authorities, plus a reference to 'public sector assurance bodies'. Scope doubt: whether this document belongs in a public-sector AI assurance map, since public bodies appear only as part of the generic 'AI supply chain'. Several passages report other bodies' work (ICO AI Auditing Framework, MHRA reforms, EU draft AI Act); these were treated as mentions. Diagrams referenced in the text were not extracted.

Title: Artificial Intelligence strategy 2026-2030
Who wrote it: European Court of Auditors (ECA)
What it is: The ECA's internal AI strategy: vision, landscape, AI governance at the ECA (AI Act correspondent, Advisory Committee on AI, AI Steering Committee), three strategic goals and nine strategic actions, with an annex of standards relevant to AI audit.
What it is for: To guide the ECA's own adoption of AI (tools for all staff, AI agents, AI-ready data, process automation, HR and administrative uses, translation) and to build its capability to audit AI used by its auditees (EU institutions and member states), while ensuring compliance with the EU AI Act and contributing to EU and international discussion.
Other important notes: Self-binding strategy of an EU institution, not legislation; operational detail is left to annual work programmes and projects approved by the AI Steering Committee. Restates EU AI Act compliance (risk classification per use case, transparency and oversight measures, conformity documentation) without citing articles; names the EDPS as market surveillance authority for AI systems. Gives the ECA a dual role: deployer of AI (internal tools, recruitment screening with human final decision by selection panels) and external auditor of AI used by auditees. Human oversight and staff accountability are stated conditions for AI in internal controls, financial administration and recruitment. No sanctions stated. Many items are options ('could', 'may') rather than commitments.

Title: Artificial Intelligence in the European Commission (AI@EC): A strategic vision to foster the development and use of lawful, safe and trustworthy Artificial Intelligence systems in the European Commission
Who wrote it: European Commission (Communication to the Commission, C(2024) 380 final)
Date: Brussels, 24 January 2024
What it is: An internal Commission communication setting a strategic vision and concrete organisational and operational actions for the Commission's own development and use of AI, with an overview of AI systems in service, in development and potential new use cases, and horizontal corporate AI enablers.
What it is for: To make the Commission an early adopter of the AI Act's risk-based approach before the Act applied, set up internal AI governance (ISG-AI, AI@EC Network, IMSB, ITCB, CMB, reporting to the College), and build operational capacity (guidelines, register of AI systems, skills, data, infrastructure, cooperation) for lawful, safe and trustworthy AI in the Commission.

Title: Guidelines for staff on the use of online available generative artificial intelligence tools
Who wrote it: European Commission. The extracted text names only 'EUROPEAN COMMISSION' in its heading; the source header (written by Claude Code, not part of the document) attributes it to the Commission's Information Management Steering Board.
Date: 2023. The text itself carries no date; the source header gives the PDF creation date as 24 May 2023.
What it is: Three-page internal staff guidance from the European Commission: a purpose and scope statement, a short explanation of generative AI, an account of four risks (unauthorised disclosure, biased and wrong answers, intellectual property, service stability), five numbered rules for staff, a conclusion, and four footnotes.
What it is for: To help Commission staff assess the risks and limitations of third-party generative AI tools that are publicly available online, and to set conditions for their safe use in Commission work.
Other important notes: NOTE (copied from the source header, as instructed): the newer version of these guidelines (3 July 2025), which is the version listed in document_selection.docx, is not available: it is known only from a release on request (asktheeu.org) and is not held. The rules mix 'must'/'shall' (Rules 1 and 4) with 'should' (Rules 2, 3 and 5), and the Conclusion reverses two of them ('Any output of generative AI models must be checked'; 'staff should never disclose non-public information or personal data'). Footnote 3 ties Rule 1 to the statutory confidentiality duty in Article 17 of the Staff Regulations and Article 339 TFEU. Applies to: all Commission staff, including statutory staff, seconded national experts and contractors or other service providers (footnote 1). Scope: third-party tools publicly available online; Commission-internal tools are excluded and left to case-by-case assessment under existing corporate IT governance.
